root_cause_hint: rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/commands.rs. Top-level dispatch correctly special-cases apply: dispatch_analyser_hook (~line 592-636) routes Hook::Apply to handle_apply_command (defined in rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/handlers.rs:909), whose doc comment (handlers.rs:883-908) explicitly states its job is to stop the generic ArgRole::Body recursion from misreading the lambda's parameter list as a command. But nested/substitution-context commands go through a separate path: run_nested_command_diagnostics (commands.rs:1515) -> collect_substitution_segments/collect_segment_recursive (commands.rs:2591-2643) -> dispatch_nested_segment (commands.rs:1651). collect_segment_recursive's generic ArgRole::Body descent (line 2631-2641) is gated only by `!definition_handler_owns_body(registry, seg.name())` (line 2632), which checks CommandSpec.definition_body — true for proc/class-definers but NOT set for apply (apply is wired via analyser_hook, not definition_body — see rust/tcl-registry/src/commands/tcl/apply.rs:56). So apply's Body-role argument (the whole lambda literal) falls through to the generic descend_command/segments_from_tree script-walk, which — exactly as the handlers.rs comment predicts — treats "{params} {body}" as one script command with cmd_name = the dequoted params-list text. Separately, dispatch_nested_segment (commands.rs:1651-1780) explicitly re-special-cases Hook::Proc and Hook::OoDefine for nested segments (lines 1763-1780) but has no arm for Hook::Apply, so even that secondary guard doesn't catch it. rust/tcl-compiler/src/analyser/diagnostics/dataflow.rs::emit_unused_variable_diagnostics (~line 538) flags a var as unused when no SSA def-use chain for it is live. Liveness comes from rust/tcl-compiler/src/ssa.rs::uses_of() (~line 1108-1192): for Statement::Barrier (which `info locals` lowers to) it only calls scan_command_words() over the barrier's own literal tokens — it has no notion that a frame-inspecting `info locals`/`info vars` enumeration followed by any dynamic per-name dereference should be treated as reading every local in scope.

The codebase already has exactly this concept, but in a sibling module that the diagnostics pipeline does not consult: rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_escape/info_subcommands.rs defines FRAME_INSPECTING_SUBCOMMANDS (includes "locals", "vars", "level", "frame", "coroutine", "errorstack") and rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_escape/cfg_propagation/handlers.rs::handle_info (~line 149-170) forces a pessimistic "escape everything" fallback whenever one of these fires. That var_escape module is wired only into inlining/var_scoping (rust/tcl-compiler/src/inlining/, rust/tcl-compiler/src/var_scoping.rs) for codegen slot-allocation correctness — grep confirms analyser/diagnostics never references var_escape. The fix is to either route the diagnostics dataflow builder through the same is_frame_inspecting_info_subcommand() check (suppressing W211 for all locals in a unit that contains a frame-inspecting `info` call), or add an equivalent barrier-escapes-all-locals rule directly in ssa.rs's uses_of()/Statement::Barrier arm.

summary: find-references is completely blind to `interp alias {} NAME {} TARGET` (matches the real pattern's `interp alias {} @ {} lindex` / `{} = {} expr`, `test/codeCoverage.tcl:17-22`). Go-to-definition and hover DO resolve the alias correctly (hover shows "Alias → lindex"/"Alias → expr", and for an alias to a user proc, definition correctly jumps through the alias to the proc), so the punctuation-lexing theory in the note is refuted — `@`/`=` are tokenized and resolved fine. The real, confirmed bug is narrower but real: references.rs never consults `analysis.command_aliases` at all, in either direction. Querying references on the alias name itself returns 0 hits (even though it has real call sites), and — more seriously — querying references on the ALIASED TARGET proc misses every call site reached only through the alias, i.e. `interp alias {} sayHi {} greet` + two `[sayHi]` calls: find-references on `greet`'s declaration returns only the proc decl and the literal "greet" word inside the `interp alias` line itself, silently omitting both real runtime call sites of `greet` (confirmed live via tclsh: `greet`'s body executes twice, printing "hi" twice). Anyone using find-references to gauge whether `greet` (or, in the real project, `lindex`/`expr`-aliased helpers) is safe to remove/rename would be told it has 0 live callers when it actually has 2.

summary: The LSP false-flags "Unknown command" (W123) for any bareword call to a command defined by a package whose pkgIndex.tcl wraps its `package ifneeded` declarations in `if {[package vsatisfies [package provide Tcl] 9.0-]} {...} else {...}` -- exactly the shape of the real georgtree_tclopt pkgIndex.tcl.in (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-tcl-lsp/b4c77bf3-47fd-5ba4-822a-000fa233bcc1/scratchpad/corpora/georgtree_tclopt/pkgIndex.tcl.in lines 5-11), the standard TEA idiom every Tcl C-extension needed after Tcl 9.0 (2024) to pick a Tcl-8-vs-9 shared library. Root cause: PackageResolver::parse_pkg_index in rust/tcl-lsp-core/src/package_resolver.rs (~lines 296-342) only recognises a `package ifneeded` command when it is literally the first words of a TOP-LEVEL command from walk_command_words(content); it never descends into a brace-delimited script body (an if/else arm), unlike its sibling collect_source_targets (~lines 231-256), which explicitly recurses through `[...]`/`{...}`/"..." wrapper words via word_unwrap(). So for an if/else-wrapped pkgIndex.tcl, parse_pkg_index returns an EMPTY Vec -- the package is completely invisible to PackageResolver, even though a byte-identical (modulo the wrapper) flat pkgIndex.tcl, or an if/else-free but equally "computed-string" nested-[list ...] body, both resolve correctly. This starves refine_w123_diagnostics (rust/tcl-lsp-server/src/lib.rs ~11417-11448, driven by refine_workspace_w123 ~11462-11484) of the package's defined-commands set, so it can never rescue the false W123 on a command the package legitimately, staticly-determinably provides. (The W120 refinement, refine_w120_diagnostics ~11304-11333, hits the same blind spot but happens to fail safe there via its conservative "unknowable" branch, so it under- rather than over-flags.) This is a "hard but not undecidable" case: both if/else branches in the real tclopt file (and in my repro) source the exact same Tcl file regardless of which runtime picked which branch, so a human -- or a resolver that recursed into if/else bodies the same way it already recurses into word wrappers -- would trivially get this right.
